                    <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 id="Abs1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number"> </span>Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>This chapter concludes the volume <i>Environmental Histories of the Dinaric Karst</i>, which examines the historical interactions between humans and the rest of nature from prehistory to the twenty-first century. The monograph at hand focuses on the most prominent features of karstic cultural landscapes, environmental conditions, and environmental change, as well as on the dynamics of the hazards and risks through time. This section provides further long-term and socio-economic history contextualisations to the environmental history data that is analysed, synthesised, interpreted, and explained in the previous chapters. This represents a starting point for a critical reflection on the environmental degradation and improvement narratives in the history of the Dinaric Karst. In the end, a selection of fundamental research desiderata is listed.</p></div></div></section>

                        <div class="main-content">
                            <section data-title="Conclusions"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec1-section"><h2 id="Sec1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">16.1 </span>Conclusions</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec1-content"><p>The Dinaric Karst is a shared yet fragmented and diversified region, as highlighted in its historical geographies and environmental histories.<sup><a href="#Fn1"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>1</a></sup> This is not only due to geomorphology, hydrology, or vegetation history but also because of some common and diverse historical conditions and cultural heritage. Therefore, the Dinaric Karst is not just a geomorphological and hydrological phenomenon or a complex physical environmental concept but also a sociocultural one.<sup><a href="#Fn2"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>2</a></sup> Its broad and complex nature and meaning inevitably require a multifaceted approach.</p><p>This volume focuses on three crucial areas of environmental history: the material and, to a lesser extent, policy-related and intellectual environmental history. As observed by John Robert McNeill, “<i>The subject matter of environmental history is often just the same as the subject matter in historical geography or historical ecology</i>”.<sup><a href="#Fn3"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>3</a></sup> This is also the case here. While some chapters rely primarily on traditional historical sources, others approach the study questions with different methodologies, in line with the research subject and the authors’ expertise.</p><p>The contents of this volume convey a variety of Dinaric Karst “stories” of the specific and often unique relations between human society and nature within the broad time span of the Anthropocene, the Age of Humans in its broadest sense.<sup><a href="#Fn4"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>4</a></sup> The present monograph discusses the impacts of several major turning points in human history, designated as the potential beginnings of the Anthropocene: the transition from hunting and gathering to agriculture, the environmental impacts of industrialisation and use of persistent industrial chemicals, and the Great Acceleration starting in the 1950s.<sup><a href="#Fn5"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>5</a></sup>
</p><p>The chapters—i.e. the case studies—deal with some of the crucial issues of environmental history and its variety of discourses: cultural landscapes holistically, i.e. the landscapes physically transformed (or altered) by human activity over time, which involves the materialisations of social or political ideologies<sup><a href="#Fn6"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>6</a></sup> (Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_2">2</a>–<a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_6">6</a>); woodland and forests (Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_7">7</a>–<a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_9">9</a>); water and climate (Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_10">10</a>–<a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_12">12</a>); and environmental degradation (Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_13">13</a>–<a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_15">15</a>). The monograph shows that the environment and people as an integral part of it are mutually dependent and co-evolve in time and space. Each human society experiences and reshapes the natural environment through culture, composed of mental and physical elements: cognitive systems, ideas, beliefs, preconceptions, values, and—more directly, through labour—tools and technology. Hence, the notion of “natural resources” is socioculturally constructed. Due to their short lifespans, people try to accumulate and often share the dynamically evolving transgenerational traditional ecological knowledge, which significantly contributes to the system’s sustainability. Though this buffer strategy worked relatively well in several ways in the preindustrial sociometabolic regime, some periods were, more markedly than others, subject to various hazards and risks to societies whose actions and interventions in their environment had uncertain outcomes.<sup><a href="#Fn7"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>7</a></sup> In the industrial sociometabolic regime, the order of magnitude of various types of human interventions in the environment increased rapidly. This was combined with the abandonment of species-rich agroecosystems of traditional landscapes dependent on labour-intensive agriculture. These processes brought about fundamental environmental transformations, including serious hazards and increased risks in some cases. The story of creosote and the hazardous environmental legacy of the historical industrial sociometabolic regime in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as presented in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_13">13</a>, the industrial karst water pollution in Bela Krajina (Slovenia) in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_14">14</a>, the massive military fuel explosion and fire in a sensitive cave environment (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_15">15</a>), and the magnified fire risk (Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5">5</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_6">6</a>) are among striking examples.</p><p>Information on historical cultural landscapes is often traceable in situ and in archival sources; the former becomes increasingly apparent with the advance of the relevant technologies. The benefits thereof are also used for discovering “hidden landscapes”. This is an analytic term for many archaeological sites, i.e. remnants of cultural landscapes, which used to be inaccessible or non-evident. In the Dinaric Karst, this was usually due to the ecological succession or fairly low relief contrast between the preserved remnants and the surrounding landscape, but can now be explored using new, non-invasive terrain survey methods, GIS, and geosciences,<sup><a href="#Fn8"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>8</a></sup> as presented in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a> and in the following subsection <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="#Sec2">16.2</a>.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Additional Contextualisations of the Book Contents"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec2-section"><h2 id="Sec2" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">16.2 </span>Additional Contextualisations of the Book Contents</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec2-content"><p>As stated in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a>, most contributions in this volume focus on the northern Dinaric Karst. Half of them—Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_2">2</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_8">8</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_10">10</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_11">11</a>, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_12">12</a>—deal with the Kras Plateau as the main focus or one of the areas under consideration. As the Kras Plateau is simultaneously the region that, for intellectual history reasons, gave the name to the processes of rock dissolution and the resulting landforms and groundwater systems worldwide (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a>), the following selection of fresh insights focuses on the Plateau and the Dinaric Karst in its surroundings.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec3"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">16.2.1 </span>Three Strongest Phases of Human Landscape Reorganisation in the Northern Dinaric Karst</h3><p>Chapters <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_2">2</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_3">3</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5">5</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_6">6</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_7">7</a>, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_8">8</a> discuss the history of land use and land cover in the Dinaric Karst. Studies in the northern Dinaric Karst identified late prehistory as <b>the first among the most fundamental phases of human landscape reorganisation</b> (Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_3">3</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a>). On the Kras Plateau, the Bronze Age of roughly the second half of the third and the second millennium BCE produced the second most open cultural landscape ever (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a>). This general finding should not obscure the fact that, due to the transformations in settlement and land-use distribution patterns through time, the Bronze-Age or Iron-Age agricultural land use in the vicinity of certain hillforts was the most intensive in history (see also Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a>). In the north-westernmost Dinaric Karst, (fortified) hilltop settlements were founded during the Bronze Age and Early Iron Age; the latter started in this area around 800 BCE.<sup><a href="#Fn9"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>9</a></sup> At that time, hillforts were a widespread settlement type in the Dinaric Karst.<sup><a href="#Fn10"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>10</a></sup> In general, the Early Iron Age in the region of today’s south-western Slovenia was characterised by “<i>economic development, rise of hillforts, population growth</i>[,] <i>and marked social stratification</i>ˮ. The region’s Iron-Age hillfort communities participated in trade with Pannonia, the Dinaric Alps, the Eastern Alps, and the Apennine Peninsula—the central and northern Italian centres, for instance. The hillfort communities reached a significant demographic peak in the fifth-to-fourth century BCE.<sup><a href="#Fn11"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>11</a></sup> The population density in these hillforts appears to have declined later but was considerable again in the waning Late Iron Age, mid-second to first-century BCE. Some hillfort regions in the northern Dinaric Karst, for example, the one along a ten-kilometre ridge between Šilentabor (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig1">16.1</a>) in the north and the eastern hinterland of Ilirska Bistrica in the south, were characterised by settlement continuity until the Late Antiquity.<sup><a href="#Fn12"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>12</a></sup> The formation of hillfort communities in the Late Bronze and especially the Early Iron Age “<i>probably went hand in hand with the development of … agricultural and pastoral</i> [agrokarst] <i>landscape</i>ˮ.<sup><a href="#Fn13"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>13</a></sup> At several places in the Dinaric Karst, agricultural land belonging to late-prehistoric hilltop settlements was located at places that are currently no longer used for agriculture.<sup><a href="#Fn14"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>14</a></sup> A hidden late-prehistoric cultural landscape has been well preserved around several hillforts between Šilentabor and the eastern hinterland of Ilirska Bistrica, as established by a detailed LiDAR-based digital elevation model and archaeological fieldwork. Figure <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig1">16.1</a> shows structures such as linear earthworks, parallel banks, and enclosures as integral parts of the multi-period, largely late-prehistoric (mainly Iron Age, partly Late-Bronze-Age) agrokarst landscape palimpsest, which evolved gradually. They are the legacy of the labour-intensive agriculture of the agrarian sociometabolic regime’s controlled solar-energy system. The age of the sampled structures was confirmed by prehistoric pottery shards. The land surface structures include arrangements associated with field cultivation (hoe farming) and livestock farming, which involved pasture enclosures and, possibly, hay meadows cleared of stone, potentially also arboriculture. An excavated bank revealed that it was not a simple clearance cairn but rather a mixture of soil and stones, so some banks and linear earthworks might have offered deeper soil layers for cultivars, sites less prone to summer drought.<sup><a href="#Fn15"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>15</a></sup> In the High and Late Middle Ages, villages that still exist nowadays were not located on hilltops in this area. Farm settlements were founded at lower elevations, while the traces of the late-prehistory-to-antiquity agrokarst landscape on shallow soils on the slopes below the hillfort ruins often belonged to outfield grasslands.<sup><a href="#Fn16"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>16</a></sup> At some locations, for example, at the hillforts of Šilentabor and Grmada south of it or Stražica north-east of Ilirska Bistrica, the areas of the preserved legacies of late-prehistoric agrokarst landscape were used for pastures in the early nineteenth century.<sup><a href="#Fn17"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>17</a></sup> Thus, land use in these marginal areas was more labour-intensive at the peak of the demographic and economic developments in the Early Iron Age than in the early nineteenth century, an era characterised by a very high agricultural density (see below in this subsection). In this case, transitions in human activities represented one of the crucial drivers of agroecosystem change in the long term. It remains to be seen whether the intensity of land use on the slopes below Šilentabor reached the late-prehistoric magnitude during the late medieval and Early Modern temporary uses of the large hillfort located in the same place as the late-prehistoric one, a shelter for the inhabitants from thirteen villages in the broader surroundings.<sup><a href="#Fn18"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>18</a></sup> However, the scarce evidence studied so far and the merely temporary character of the late medieval to Early Modern fort, excluding the few inhabitants of the castle that was erected in the hillfort site, do not support this hypothesis—fields and meadows at lower elevations were largely cultivated also when people temporarily retreated to the hillfort.<sup><a href="#Fn19"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>19</a></sup> This suggests that the late-prehistoric land use there was indeed most intensive.</p><div Many of the structures, which were located in pastures in the early nineteenth century and cannot be identified as fences around meadows and cultivated fields existing in that period or as present structures, are remnants of this landscape’s most intensive prehistoric agricultural use. <i>Sources</i> as noted in the Figure; the map in the middle: own elaboration</p></div></div><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="chapter-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_16/figures/1" data-track-dest="link:Figure1 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 1" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<p>Similar examples can be found at some other hillforts in the broader region<sup><a href="#Fn20"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>20</a></sup>: a comparison between the LiDAR-based insights into the hidden prehistoric landscape in the left central section of Fig. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4.4</a> and the early-nineteenth-century land use in the same area<sup><a href="#Fn21"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>21</a></sup> reveals many structures on the slopes of this marginal area—not only enclosures but also field boundaries as legacies of agricultural practices, more intensive than simple grazing in the area used as a pasture in the early nineteenth century (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a>). Since the High Middle Ages, examples of land use more intensive than in the early nineteenth century have been only exceptional and limited to a few permanently deserted villages and places where farmers could not cope with water and wind erosion in the cultivated fields, which they therefore abandoned.<sup><a href="#Fn22"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>22</a></sup>
</p><p><b>The second, Early Modern phase of landscape reorganisation</b> as a consequence of a substantial increase in agricultural density is presented in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a> based on the soil accumulation in <i>dolines</i>. These results are fundamental and relevant in the broad Dinaric Karst context, so they need to be embedded in the economic and social history processes proven by written sources to integrate environmental history into the total history frame.<sup><a href="#Fn23"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>23</a></sup>
</p><p>In the Late Middle Ages, until around the fourteenth century, the Kras Plateau was most likely covered by relatively extensive forests next to some agricultural land. Archival sources match palynological results indicating a medieval expansion of oak forests.<sup><a href="#Fn24"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>24</a></sup> Namely, during the Late Middle Ages, the Kras Plateau was severely depopulated for many reasons, such as the broader economic conditions in Europe, epidemics, harvest failures, military incursions from the expanding Ottoman Empire, the War of the League of Combrai (1508–1516), or emigration to urban settlements,<sup><a href="#Fn25"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>25</a></sup> for example, the Venetian coastal town of Koper (It. <i>Capodistria</i>), by far the largest urban settlement in the vicinity and one of the largest towns along the eastern Adriatic coast with some 7000–10,000 inhabitants from the Late Middle Ages to the mid-sixteenth century,<sup><a href="#Fn26"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>26</a></sup> or the Habsburg port of Trieste, a town of considerable size, though much smaller than Koper at the time.<sup><a href="#Fn27"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>27</a></sup> In the seigneury of Senožeče (the central settlement is located on the eastern Kras Plateau), roughly 40% of farms were uninhabited as recorded in 1531—a percentage representative of the broader area and a result of the processes lasting for more than a century, including the severe demographic losses between the late 1460s and 1531. Most empty farms were used as extensively managed grasslands, while a minority were completely abandoned.<sup><a href="#Fn28"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>28</a></sup> In the era of late medieval and early-sixteenth-century depopulation, quite a lot of forests were located on the Kras Plateau.<sup><a href="#Fn29"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>29</a></sup> By the second half of the sixteenth century, the demographic conditions recovered in a period of strengthened political stability, and, therefore, a significant increase in the number of farm households compared to the time before the late-medieval crisis began. Simultaneously, on the increasingly populated Kras Plateau, another relevant farming institution was founded in 1580: the princely stud farm in Lipica, a new local and regional economic and environmental actor, which significantly raised the demand for grassland resources. In the second half of the 1610s, the Lipica stud farm kept about 150–200 mares, foals, and stallions, and significantly more at the peak of the early seventeenth century. The number then decreased due to the 1625 stud farm reform. In diverse stages, the general trend of the increasing agricultural density on the Kras Plateau and the growing number of smallholdings continued until the nineteenth century. This led to land-use intensification, for example, the conversion of pastures and forests to meadows, vineyards, and cultivated fields as of the sixteenth century, which were often situated in marginal environmental conditions. Thus, even though villages on the Kras Plateau originate from the Middle Ages, the magnified Early Modern agricultural density, in interaction with natural processes and living beings, created an incomparably more open cultural landscape than medieval colonisation. These processes belonged to the widespread deforestation in the (Sub)Mediterranean environments in the early modern Europe, including the (Sub)Mediterranean areas of the Dinaric Karst. However, it is important to emphasise that the rising population numbers were not directly linked to the increase in farmland: not only were the farming orientations and the economic standard not constant through time, but the integrated peasant economy also involved several kinds of agricultural and non-agrarian income. In the case of the Kras Plateau, the latter included the mesoregional trade with Habsburg and Venetian port towns in northern Istria, crafts, temporary jobs in urban settlements, etc. Thus, the pressure of labour-intensive agriculture on farmland rose particularly heavily in times of economic depression in the non-agricultural economy. Nonetheless, the broader trade conditions, like the demand in the rapidly growing Trieste, the Habsburg Monarchy’s main port in the mercantilist eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, also resulted in strengthened market-oriented agriculture on the Kras Plateau.<sup><a href="#Fn30"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>30</a></sup>
</p><p>An approximate comparison of livestock recorded in eight villages between the Kras Plateau east of Trieste (Vrhpolje) and Črni Kal east of Koper (Capodistria) in 1627 and in 1955 (or 1948), most of which are located on limestone karst, shows a considerable increase in the number of total livestock held at farms in these villages. The approximate number of livestock units in the mid-twentieth century (about 967) amounted to approximately 235% of the one officially inventoried in 1627 (around 411), with huge differences between villages. In the same interval, the number of holdings more than doubled (from 135 to 302). In addition, within this chronological interval, the livestock size expanded significantly, so the environmental impacts of the rising livestock numbers were even greater. Nonetheless, it is clear that several farms did not keep as many of their own livestock as they could in 1627 because several domestic animals perished due to an infectious disease, a severe bora storm that killed tens of domestic animals in a pasture, etc. In 1627, these farmers thus also reared some foreign livestock owned by burghers or other farmers, for example.<sup><a href="#Fn31"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>31</a></sup> It is also likely that some livestock was hidden in 1627. Therefore, it seems that the inventoried livestock numbers did not fully reach the carrying capacity of the 1627 cultural landscape. All in all, the livestock present in the mid-twentieth century most likely demanded significantly more fodder than the 1627 cultural landscape could deliver, but not as much more as the figures presented would suggest. We should add that in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, cattle replaced sheep in most places on the Kras Plateau due to several economic factors. The development of the global wool and cotton market and raised milk demand in Trieste were important elements in this process.<sup><a href="#Fn32"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>32</a></sup> One of the main landscape impacts of the transition from sheep to cattle on the Kras Plateau was an increased stone clearing in pastures where sheep and some old cattle breeds could graze, while the pastures were unsuitable for modern cattle breeds. Stone clearing was also a consequence of the frequent land-use change from pastures to hay meadows, namely more hay was required because cattle was not involved in the transhumance and the role of barn-feeding in cattle husbandry strengthened.<sup><a href="#Fn33"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>33</a></sup> Looking deeper into the relevant history, Early Modern sheep farming on the Kras Plateau, like in most of the Dinaric Karst, was market oriented to a significant degree. Despite the meagre appearance of the species-rich dry calcareous grasslands and low yield quantities, they provided quality, aromatic fodder, which resulted in tasty meat. Thus, the lambs from the Kras Plateau were massively exported to Venice, where they reached exceptionally high prices, as observed in 1780<sup><a href="#Fn34"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>34</a></sup>—an evidence of how the considerable demand co-shaped the local economy. Cereals from this plateau also had their merits—granted, the grains were usually small, but the seed hull was thin and the quantity of flour per unit of grains was high, ensuring a considerable wheat market price. Namely, despite the limited surfaces suitable for field cultivation on the Kras Plateau, resulting in regular cereal purchases to fulfil the needs of many households, significant wheat quantities from the plateau were regularly sold, as the landlords or tithe lords sold much of the rent they had received in wheat dues. Later, farmers would sell their wheat surplus directly, while their daily diet was based on cheaper cereals.<sup><a href="#Fn35"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>35</a></sup>
</p><p>The accelerated Early Modern soil erosion, demonstrated in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a> based on the <i>doline</i> infills near Divača, reflects, on the one hand, the soil erosion in the grasslands, especially overgrazed ones, leading, for instance, to a gradual increase in barren karst (see below). On the other hand, soil erosion in cultivated fields was also intense. In addition to the expanding grasslands and agricultural fields, the high soil erosion rates in the Early Modern period resulted from the increasingly marginal site conditions in the areas where farming was introduced or land use intensified in the context of the Early Modern farming expansion (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a>).<sup><a href="#Fn36"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>36</a></sup> The Little Ice Age climate might have also contributed to higher soil erosion rates. The regular appearance of stones in agricultural land, caused by pluvial and wind erosion and mitigated by the occasionally repeated stone removal from the fields and the transport of the eroded soil back to the plots of its origin, was usually observed in many Dinaric Karst regions with agriculture on shallow or rocky soils—farmers in various places of the macroregion, including the Kras Plateau, used to say that “<i>stones grow</i>”.<sup><a href="#Fn37"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>37</a></sup> The removed rocks were used for dry stone walls or deposited in clearance cairns (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a>). Soil erosion in the cultivated fields on shallow soils that covered gentle slopes was so strong that the soil had to be collected in the depressions and transported back to the fields after heavy rain as well as regularly, every second or third year, to keep the land productive for field crops in times of labour-intensive agriculture of the agrarian sociometabolic regime’s controlled solar-energy system. This process was mitigated by terraces and walls stabilising the soil that farmers had brought to some locations to create fields artificially.<sup><a href="#Fn38"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>38</a></sup>
</p><p>In the global context of karst macroregions, the geological composition of the Dinaric Karst is exceptionally complex.<sup><a href="#Fn39"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>39</a></sup> This volume therefore deals with several different karst environments, as outlined in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a>. Even on the Kras Plateau, a connection between environmental and social conditions resulted in two agricultural regions on the plateau in the last centuries (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig2">16.2</a>). The “<i>Teran</i> Kras” is named after the local red wine called <i>teran</i>. In the Early Modern Period, it was intended for local consumption and the mesoregional market, as it was not as highly appreciated as quality white wines. During the nineteenth century, the attitude towards <i>teran</i> changed: it became highly valued in the city of Trieste and has remained a prized wine variety ever since. In the early nineteenth century, the open or wooded, often rocky pastures, primarily used for sheep grazing, covered more than half of the <i>Teran</i> Kras, with significant differences in the percentage of pastures in the total agricultural land at the village level.<sup><a href="#Fn40"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>40</a></sup> Nonetheless, the <i>Teran</i> Kras was characterised by a significantly higher percentage of cultivated fields and vineyards than the so-called Grassland Kras, i.e. the other agricultural region on the plateau. The considerable share of wood meadows in the <i>Teran</i> Kras delivered higher grassland yields than the open meadows in the local environment. Wood meadows also produced wood, acorn for pigs, ash-leaf hay (mainly for sheep), and leaf litter for bedding. The tree shade alleviated the summer drought, resulting in denser grassland, while fallen leaves contributed to nutrient cycling in the meadow agroecosystem.<sup><a href="#Fn41"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>41</a></sup> Wood meadows have a long tradition there: in the 1630s, the care for the high-quality grassland and the good condition of the oak stand in the local wood meadow was recorded in the sources regarding the Lipica stud farm.<sup><a href="#Fn42"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>42</a></sup> In some areas of the <i>Teran</i> Kras, meadows were so extensive and haymaking so labour-intensive that the locals had to rely on an external haymaking workforce, at least in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries—similarly to some sections of the Grassland Kras, as presented below. One such example was the cadastral municipality of Tomaj (see its central settlement in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig2">16.2</a>), where hay meadows, most of them wooded, covered the majority of the territory in the early nineteenth century; the microregion of Tomaj is highly fertile for agriculture in the broader Kras context. Only 7% of the 346 ha of hay meadows in the cadastral municipality of Tomaj, however, allowed for mowing by scythe only. Elsewhere, the rocks were not entirely cleared, so haymakers would use scythes as well as sickles (47% of the meadows) or had to cut the meadow plants using sickles only (46% of the meadows).<sup><a href="#Fn43"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>43</a></sup>
</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-2" data-title="Fig. 16.2"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig2" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 16.2</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><a class="c-article-section__figure-link" data-test="img-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="image" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_16/figures/2" rel="nofollow"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-56089-7_16/MediaObjects/500207_1_En_16_Fig2_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="Fig2" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-56089-7_16/MediaObjects/500207_1_En_16_Fig2_HTML.png" alt="A map of the Kras plateau in Europe that is pattern-coded. The marked legends are Teran Karst Landscape, Grassland Karst Landscape, Karstic Rocks, and Non-Karstic Rocks." loading="lazy" width="685" height="979"></picture></a><p class="c-article-section__figure-credit text-right c-article-section__figure-credit-right" data-test="figure-credit"><i>Source</i> Own elaboration, adapted from Moritsch (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1969" title="" href="#ref-CR67" id="ref-link-section-d7135060e1848">1969</a>), Karte 10</p></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-2-desc"><p>Two main agricultural regions on the Kras Plateau: the “<i>Teran</i> Kras” and the “Grassland Kras”.</p></div></div><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="chapter-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_16/figures/2" data-track-dest="link:Figure2 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 2" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<p>The Grassland Kras, characterised by a meagre percentage of cultivated fields, covered the plateau’s south-eastern, north-western, and western parts (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig2">16.2</a>). The Divača Kras, where soil samples referred to in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a> were taken, belongs to this type of Kras. The Grassland Kras was characterised by a high percentage of pastures and hay meadows. Pastures, including some barren land, covered about 70% of the area. Barren rocks were less common in the Grassland Kras at higher elevations than at lower altitudes. In the cadastral municipality of Divača (see its central settlement in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig2">16.2</a>), most hay meadows needed to be cut by sickle. As the hay meadows were so extensive, seasonal workers from the Upper Soča valley (today north-western Slovenia), located in the south-eastern Alps more than forty kilometres away, as well as those from some not so distant parts were usually hired to help with haymaking, as reported for the south-east of the Grassland Kras in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Hay from several parts of the Grassland Kras (see the surroundings of Senožeče in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_10">10</a>) would be sold in the coastal urban settlements and villages, an activity which had started centuries before the Habsburg Monarchy built the railway connection between Vienna and Trieste in 1857 (see Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a>).<sup><a href="#Fn44"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>44</a></sup>
</p><p>In several parts of both the Grassland and <i>Teran</i> Kras, the local demand for hay was reduced by transhumance. Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a> emphasises that transhumance used to be a common practice in the agricultural history of the Dinaric Karst in the <i>longue durée</i> perspective. A recent cultural landscape history synthesis on the Kras Plateau underestimated its local significance in the Early Modern Period but rightly emphasised the potential changes in the presence and trends of transhumance involving Kras through time.<sup><a href="#Fn45"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>45</a></sup> In the Early Modern Period and later, transhumance linked several diverse parts of the Kras Plateau (elevations between 200 and 500 m ASL) and the summer pastures on the high Dinaric Karst plateaus or their slopes—e.g. Nanos (about 1200 m ASL) and probably Javorniki (similarly, with the highest peaks at about 1200 m ASL) and Snežnik (even higher)—the Vremščica Hill (about 1000 m ASL), as well as some parts of the Kras Plateau and the lowland winter pastures in Istria (nowadays located in south-western Slovenia and north-western Croatia) and Friuli (today in north-eastern Italy). It is, however, clear that a lot (or most) of livestock overwintered on the Kras Plateau.<sup><a href="#Fn46"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>46</a></sup> Historical transhumance involving sheep and goats from the plateau deserves further research attention.</p><p><b>The third fundamental phase of human-induced landscape reorganisation started in the late nineteenth century</b>, with extensive afforestation projects: initially, the black pine plantations on the Kras Plateau, followed by further examples in several other places of the Dinaric Karst. Focusing on the forest transition on the Kras Plateau and in many other Dinaric Karst regions, the afforestation was coupled with the ecological succession due to deagrarianisation. These processes are presented in Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_8">8</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5">5</a>, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_6">6</a>, which focus also on the socio-economic triggers and environmental consequences.<sup><a href="#Fn47"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>47</a></sup> Another crucial aspect of this landscape transformation phase, mainly since the second half of the twentieth century, is the industrialised farming intensification in times of the Great Acceleration, contributing its share to the losses of species-rich agroecosystems and causing serious environmental degradation. However, the spatial scale of this process differs significantly from one Dinaric Karst mesoregion to the other. While the intensive industrialised farming has, to a certain degree, affected the agroecosystems in all the regions where the farming has not ceased, its impacts in several areas with considerable karstic environmental constraints on farming, such as the Kras Plateau<sup><a href="#Fn48"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>48</a></sup> or most of the Dalmatian karst (Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5">5</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_6">6</a>), have been much less profound than in some other Dinaric Karst regions that are more favourable for or more easily adapted to modern intensive farming (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_14">14</a>).<sup><a href="#Fn49"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>49</a></sup>
</p><p>The processes presented here have had a diverse and extensive impact on the contents of this volume. For instance, the network of aquatic and wetland ecosystems of artificial waterbodies on the Kras Plateau changed thoroughly exactly when it was heavily populated by livestock and people and the agricultural density was enormous<sup><a href="#Fn50"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>50</a></sup> (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_11">11</a>). The prevalent local smallholders struggled to cope with the subsistence crisis of the mid-1860s in a heavily used environment. Hence, many farmers were forced to look elsewhere for work—often in the port city of Trieste and some in the distant forests of what is now northern Croatia and elsewhere (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_10">10</a>). Due to climate change with increasing aridity, altered river beds, and higher evapotranspiration because of the expansion of forests, the persistence of the northern Dinaric Karst floods of 1864 is difficult to imagine today (compare Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_10">10</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_12">12</a>).</p><p>Modern karst explorations began in the Dinaric Karst (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a>) when it was more or less at its barest and when the surface karst phenomena were therefore most obvious.<sup><a href="#Fn51"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>51</a></sup> At that time, these phenomena were thus incomparably more noticeable in the landscape than today, more than a century after the massive afforestation with black pine and the relevant ecological succession. This is yet another example of the complex interactions between the natural processes and human society (Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5">5</a>–<a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_8">8</a>), which brings our attention to the environmental degradation and improvement narratives in the Dinaric Karst’s history or the topic of the subsection <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="#Sec4">16.2.2</a>.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec4"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">16.2.2 </span>The Reconsidered Environmental Degradation and Improvement Narratives</h3><p>On the one hand, instead of an unreflected “<i>lament over loss and damage as people did awful things to flora, fauna and the land</i> […], <i>a more mature examination of a wider, more complex range of relationships with the rest of the nature</i>” became characteristic for the global mainstream environmental history research.<sup><a href="#Fn52"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>52</a></sup> On the other hand, historiographical narratives of humans-induced environmental “improvement” that followed the historical scientific and policy discourse need to be reconsidered (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_8">8</a>).<sup><a href="#Fn53"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>53</a></sup> Both approaches were applied in the recent environmental historiography of the Kras Plateau.</p><p>Considering the degradation narratives in scientific writing, this text focuses on the history of barren karst. Barren rocky ground was characteristic of some sections of the Dinaric Karst, mainly on Adriatic islands, the Adriatic-facing mountain slopes, and the various lowlands in the Dalmatian hinterland (Zagora), as observed in Early Modern administrative records and scientific writing.<sup><a href="#Fn54"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>54</a></sup> There, grassland plants were often limited to depressions in karren. Barrenness resulted from the interactions between unsustainable forest uses (forest fires, sometimes excessive felling) and overgrazing in a sensitive agrokarst grassland or forest environment. In Dalmatia, with its Mediterranean climate, regular summer droughts and fierce, dry bora wind gusts that easily blow away the topsoil (especially on the islands facing the main bora corridors; see Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_7">7</a>), the barren area was larger, and the degree of the landscape’s barrenness at the sites most void of vegetation was somewhat higher than on the Kras Plateau.<sup><a href="#Fn55"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>55</a></sup> However, apart from the natural environmental conditions and the general course of agricultural and forest history, the centuries-long Early Modern border position (between the Ottoman, Venetian, and Habsburg territories) significantly influenced the Dalmatian karst in the environmental-historical sense, as it contributed to the lack of possibilities for continuous resource management and the unsustainable use of the scarce resources (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5">5</a>). In the Early Modern Period, the borderland position in Dalmatia resulted in wars, frequent border changes until the early eighteenth century, insecurity for persistent sedentary settlement, migrations, and favoured migratory pastoralism on the mainland. Unsurprisingly, the barren area in the Dalmatian hinterland (Zagora) was most likely larger in the early eighteenth century than in the times of Cvijić’s fieldwork almost two centuries after the end of the Ottoman–Venetian wars. For the islands, the political instability until the early eighteenth century meant the influx of settlers from the war-torn mainland and thus heavier environmental pressure on arable land, hoed parcels, pastures, vineyards, olive groves, and woodlands in terms of more labour-intensive uses and, in several places, intensification of the land-use categories. These processes contributed to the expansion of barren areas, especially in the pasture commons.<sup><a href="#Fn56"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>56</a></sup>
</p><p>However, at least in some parts of the Dinaric Karst, such as the Kras Plateau, barren land became a topos, and its extent was presented in an exaggerated manner.<sup><a href="#Fn57"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>57</a></sup> This topos still appears in recent karstology publications.<sup><a href="#Fn58"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>58</a></sup> In addition to the rocky topos, coppice—which produced firewood, vineyard stakes, tree-leaf hay, and grassland plants—and (pollarded) solitary trees were interpreted as a massively degraded agroenvironment in accordance with the historical forestry science standards that opposed traditional agroforestry uses, including those that maintained the species-rich wooded ecosystems in the long term and provided (most of) the wood needed in the local economy. In fact, the Early Modern records attest to extensive traditional ecological knowledge that ensured functional and often relatively sustainable uses of such agroecosystems on the Kras Plateau. These were thoroughly different from natural forests but were nevertheless species-rich. Therefore, such a transformed species-rich environment that enabled economic uses in the context of labour-intensive agriculture of the agrarian sociometabolic regime’s controlled solar-energy system cannot be deemed as degradation. Around 1830, when the deforestation of the Kras Plateau was at its worst, wooded grasslands and forests—i.e. land with at least some woody vegetation (excluding vineyards and orchards)—covered one-third of Kras (forests grew on 13% of the plateau). Moreover, open pastures covered another 38% of the surface, and open meadows represented 7%. Altogether, only these land-use categories covered 76% of the landscape. Granted, many of the pastures and some of the meadows were exceedingly rocky: in the cadastral municipality of Divača—as an example of a microregion with an exceptionally high percentage of barren karst in the very south of its territory in the broader Kras context—pastures delivering only a quarter of the usual amount of grazing resources due to the vast rocky area covered almost three quarters of the territory in early nineteenth century (see the central settlement in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig2">16.2</a>).<sup><a href="#Fn59"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>59</a></sup> The soil erosion leading to such conditions is also reflected in the analysed <i>doline</i> infills—several sampling sites yielding the results presented in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_4">4</a> are located exactly there.<sup><a href="#Fn60"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>60</a></sup> This was one of the barren karst microregions on the Kras Plateau often observed by visitors, as it was crossed by the old commercial road from Vienna to Trieste that was improved in the mercantilist eighteenth century. Since 1857, the area under consideration was located near the Divača station of the Vienna–Trieste railway; since 1876, this barren karst was crossed by the railroad connection from Vienna to Pula (southern Istria, today in Croatia).<sup><a href="#Fn61"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>61</a></sup> The impressions from this region must have contributed to the notion of Kras as a barren, stony landscape. Nonetheless, the Kras Plateau as a whole has never been a rocky desert where agricultural land would be largely confined to the “oases” in <i>dolines</i>.<sup><a href="#Fn62"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>62</a></sup> Even the cadastral municipality of Divača sold some hay to the coastal settlements, as recorded in the early nineteenth century.<sup><a href="#Fn63"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>63</a></sup> During the hot and dry summer weather, resulting in the desolate appearance of grasslands and the absence of surface water, visitors felt as if they had been travelling around a desert-like, rocky environment.<sup><a href="#Fn64"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>64</a></sup> Meanwhile, the cultivated fields located in <i>dolines</i> were mostly out of sight of casual travellers,<sup><a href="#Fn65"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>65</a></sup> who thus often had an impression of a landscape that was very different from reality. While hay scarcity called for hay purchases in several cadastral municipalities on the Kras Plateau, the following further evidence proves that the historical agroecosystems on several parts of the plateau were comparatively healthy: vast quantities of hay were sold from some parts of the region of Grassland Kras (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig2">16.2</a>); the agroecosystems supported large numbers of sheep; and from a fairly limited part of the plateau, even firewood was sold to Trieste, as recorded in the nineteenth century, at the peak of the Kras Plateau’s deforestation.<sup><a href="#Fn66"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>66</a></sup>
</p><p>Another example of agroecosystems in the northern Dinaric Karst, which are usually considered degraded, are the leaf litter forests of Bela Krajina, a region now located in south-eastern Slovenia. In the <i>longue durée</i> perspective, these socio-natural sites<sup><a href="#Fn67"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>67</a></sup> were altered by the labour-intensive agriculture. The resulting ecosystems are characterised by distinct species compositions (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_14">14</a>). Litter raking in these environments started way back in the controlled solar-energy system of the agrarian sociometabolic regime and intensified in the eighteenth and the nineteenth centuries, when the role of barn-keeping in livestock husbandry increased. Forest litter raking mostly ceased in the second half of the twentieth century with the spread of other livestock bedding types, the introduction of slatted barn floor, or the abandonment of livestock farming. In the long run, litter raking changed the forest ecosystems, mainly due to the regular removal of nutrients. Nonetheless, with several protected species occurring there—for example, the <i>Helleborus dumetorum</i> hellebore species, stag’s-horn clubmoss (<i>Lycopodium clavatum</i>), sweet william (<i>Dianthus barbatus</i>), and European cyclamen (<i>Cyclamen purpurascens</i>)—the existent litter forests are nowadays considered ecosystem types worth preserving for biodiversity reasons, at least in limited landscape sections. Soil acidification as a consequence of litter-raking created more favorable site conditions for stag’s-horn clubmoss, an organism occuring only at acidic, nutrient poor sites (Aeschimann et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="" href="#ref-CR1" id="ref-link-section-d7135060e2497">2004</a>).<sup><a href="#Fn68"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>68</a></sup> Thus, following the traditional-forestry-science-inspired narrative of a degraded environment of litter forests is not the only option (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_14">14</a>). The plurality of possible interpretations results from more than one sensible ecological baseline set as the reference point.<sup><a href="#Fn69"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>69</a></sup> On the one hand, the increased soil acidity and decreased nutrient availability reduced the species diversity and created conditions less fertile for many plants, which had grown there prior to the litter raking.<sup><a href="#Fn70"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>70</a></sup> However, on the other hand, this allowed for an increased abundance of other organisms occurring in the “traditional” cultural landscape of the nineteenth century and earlier, including the listed rare species.</p><p>Focusing on the narratives of improvement, the classic karstology literature claims that the project of the afforestation of the Kras Plateau with black pine, taking place in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, the Kingdom of Italy, and the socialist Yugoslavia (see the contexts in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_8">8</a>) between the late-nineteenth and the mid-twentieth century, “<i>was long-lasting and successful, resulting in the selection of appropriate species, the development of new techniques for planting, and for the protection of plantations. It was influential in forestry practice elsewhere in Europe</i>”.<sup><a href="#Fn71"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>71</a></sup> Such discourse was inspired by historical forestry science.<sup><a href="#Fn72"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>72</a></sup> In fact, the afforestation of the Kras Plateau with black pine in Austria-Hungary was the first extensive afforestation project in the (Sub-)Mediterranean, as established by Alfred Thomas Grove and Oliver Rackham. It inspired several subsequent afforestation projects (see also Chaps. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5">5</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_7">7</a>).<sup><a href="#Fn73"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>73</a></sup> It did establish forests in grasslands and even in previously barren land, where soil was brought in the framework of that project. Nonetheless, the afforestation with a non-native species that became naturalised in Kras opened up new and unforeseen long-term challenges in the interaction between humans and the rest of nature. These included the following: insecticide application in the sensitive karst environments in the framework of the afforestation; pine processionary moth infestation; the environmental impacts of the chemical suppression of organisms perceived as pests in pine stands; consequences for human health resulting from pine processionary moth suppression; unfulfilled expectations regarding the black pine’s impact on the soil; the increased fire risk in pine forests; the influences of the altered land use on the local farm economy; and decreased biodiversity in the monoculture black pine plantations (Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_8">8</a>). “<i>From today’s point of view, the planting of alien tree species, despite preventing further soil erosion, is considered an inappropriate measure by most ecologists and many foresters</i>.”<sup><a href="#Fn74"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>74</a></sup> However, the holistic picture of the afforestation projects’ environmental impacts at the various Dinaric Karst sites differed significantly, even where the same tree species was involved. In the case of the southern slopes of the Svilaja Mountain in the Dalmatian hinterland (Zagora) during the 1960s in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the black pine that was planted was an autochthonous species there, and the goal was to stop and prevent excessive flooding in one of the most important fertile areas of Mućko Polje after the unsustainable use of resources, deforestation, and subsequent massive erosion.<sup><a href="#Fn75"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>75</a></sup>
</p><p>The examples given here focus on the barren land and forest. However, several other environmental histories of the Dinaric Karst deserve a similar holistic perspective. This topic brings us to the last subsection.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Paving the Way for Future Research: From the Local to the Global Perspective"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec5-section"><h2 id="Sec5" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">16.3 </span>Paving the Way for Future Research: From the Local to the Global Perspective</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec5-content"><p>As explained in Chap. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_1">1</a>, this volume is the first multiauthored inter- and multidisciplinary monograph on the history of the Dinaric Karst environments and the local interactions between society and nature, spanning several historical periods. Thus, several gaps remain that will need to be bridged in the future.</p><p>Since this book focuses on material, some policy-related, and some intellectual environmental history, the fourth main environmental history study field—cultural environmental history<sup><a href="#Fn76"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>76</a></sup>—largely remains a desideratum, along with further material, policy, and intellectual environmental history studies. A few Early Modern examples of cultural history data on the northern Dinaric Karst caves are briefly presented. In some parts of the Dinaric Karst, people would regularly get water from caves, for example, at Bločice east of Cerknica Polje (today in Slovenia), a place that will be mentioned again below. At many other locations, they would descend to the water in caves in times of drought.<sup><a href="#Fn77"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>77</a></sup> Farmers also visited the caves below the bottoms of intermittent lakes in some karst <i>poljes</i> to fish or merely collect the fish that got stuck there when the water was sinking—full cartloads in some cases. Regular cave visits, however, did not mean that the fear of the karstic underground world vanished.<sup><a href="#Fn78"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>78</a></sup> We can all imagine the monsters appearing on the cave walls and speleothems in the flickering light and shadows as the visitors found their way to the water carrying torches.<sup><a href="#Fn79"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>79</a></sup> Visits to caves resulted in many stories of cave ghosts, such as the one allegedly reported by a man fishing in a cave below the Cerknica Polje in the seventeen century: as a thunderstorm approached and the thunder echoed in the cave, the fisherman got scared and ascended to the surface. When he returned, he found his fishing net broken and claimed a ghost had destroyed it. The endemic cave fauna—the olm (<i>Proteus anguinus</i>), a cave-dwelling salamander that occasionally appears in some karst springs—was sometimes interpreted as dragon younglings from the karst underground. Caves that were said to get annoyed if provoked and send out storms are another cultural environmental history topic, and annual blessings were held at some such caves in the early modern period and later to prevent the storms.<sup><a href="#Fn80"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>80</a></sup> The cultural history of fears of the karst underground could result in exceedingly tragic episodes such as the witch trial killing many innocent inhabitants of the village of Bločice in the seventeenth century, who reportedly claimed they had met the Devil in the caves where they supplied themselves with water.<sup><a href="#Fn81"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>81</a></sup> Witch hunts have recently received much environmental historiography attention in Central Europe, focused on the climate history perspective<sup><a href="#Fn82"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>82</a></sup>; a systematic karst-specific approach to the topic is a desideratum. A cultural history of caves can range from perceptions of fear, and their broader impacts to positive attitudes towards the karst underground, such as healing cave water springs and uses of speleothems in folk medicine. The history of some caves as holy mass sites<sup><a href="#Fn83"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>83</a></sup> could address the question of whether holding holy masses in some caves was primarily a continuation of pre-Christian cult sites,<sup><a href="#Fn84"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>84</a></sup> a sign of taming the eerie underground world, or simply a means of appreciating the beauty of the speleothem-filled caves.</p><p>Focusing on general environmental history desiderata, some authors in this volume showed remarkable talent for interdisciplinary cooperation. However, optimally, “[e]<i>nvironmental history is about as interdisciplinary as intellectual pursuits can get.</i>”<sup><a href="#Fn85"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>85</a></sup> The desire to ensure even greater interdisciplinarity is not specific to the Dinaric Karst: it has recently been emphasised by global mainstream environmental historians.<sup><a href="#Fn86"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>86</a></sup> To quote Verena Winiwarter’s response at a roundtable debate <i>Practicing interdisciplinarity in environmental history: potentials and pitfalls</i>, held at the <i>Third world congress of environmental history</i> in Florianópolis, Brazil: “<i>If you want to go fast – go alone. But, if you want to go far – go together!</i>ˮ.<sup><a href="#Fn87"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>87</a></sup>
</p><p>Another global observation that John Robert McNeill’s environmental historiography emphasises is that more inspiration by the publications written by scholars working on similar or related subjects, concepts, and methodological approaches elsewhere in the world “<i>will also propel environmental history forward</i>ˮ.<sup><a href="#Fn88"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>88</a></sup> This is particularly pressing in several texts on the Dinaric Karst. Namely, in the times when environmental historiography production is so extensive that following U.S. publications alone has become a full-time job; when environmental history is published in many languages; and when certain academic environments maintain their tradition as centres of knowledge while the achievements of diligent authors, published in states perceived as peripheral (like the Dinaric Karst countries, for example), receive much less worldwide attention, and the inadequate knowledge of some studies from other continents in the Dinaric Karst countries and of some Dinaric Karst literature abroad is sometimes a challenge.<sup><a href="#Fn89"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>89</a></sup>
</p><p>This challenge also results in a lack of a theoretical coherence within this interdisciplinary monograph. Workshops focusing on the issue at hand, participated in by all the authors involved, could have led to a higher level of theoretical consistency “<i>while maintaining the richness of various scientific approaches and flavo</i>[u]<i>rs</i>”. Nonetheless, considerable theoretical uniformity in an interdisciplinary volume tackling diverse research topics, written by several authors used to diverse epistemological frameworks, is a highly time-consuming goal even under ordinary conditions,<sup><a href="#Fn90"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>90</a></sup> let alone during the times of the COVID-19 pandemic when such an effort would have resulted in excessive delays. Hence, the decision was made to skip this stage in the first book of this kind focusing on the Dinaric Karst.</p><p>In conclusion, let us quote John Robert McNeill: “[E]<i>nvironmental history as a field needs more integration, both more integration with other disciplines, and more integration within itself, among scholars at work on different regions and different problems</i>.ˮ<sup><a href="#Fn91"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>91</a></sup> This is one of the key desiderata regarding the environmental history of the Dinaric Karst.</p></div></div></section>
